section.title: Remember His Wonderful Works
section.sectionRationale: A historical hymn in Book IV, Psalms 90 to 106, that rehearses the covenant faithfulness of God from Abraham through Jacob, Joseph, the Exodus, and the wilderness, into the gift of Canaan. Its opening verses are quoted almost verbatim in David's song at the bringing of the ark, 1 Chronicles 16:8-22, and it forms a deliberate pair with Psalm 106, which follows immediately: this psalm celebrates what God did, that psalm confesses how Israel responded.
section.thesis: The LORD who chose Abraham and swore an everlasting covenant to his offspring has kept every word of it, protecting a small wandering family, sending Joseph ahead into Egypt, humbling Pharaoh with wonders, and bringing His people out with joy into the land He promised, so that remembering His wonders is itself the fuel of praise.
section.frameNote: Eight movements: a call to praise and remember, verses 1 to 6; the everlasting covenant, verses 7 to 11; the patriarchs protected among the nations, verses 12 to 15; Joseph sent ahead into Egypt, verses 16 to 22; Israel multiplying in Egypt, verses 23 to 25; Moses, Aaron, and the plagues, verses 26 to 36; the exodus and wilderness provision, verses 37 to 41; and the land given so that Israel might keep His statutes, verses 42 to 45.

units.label: Give thanks to the LORD
units.note: a call to praise and remember

verses.text: Give thanks to the LORD, call upon His name; make known His deeds among the nations.
Sing to Him, sing praises to Him; tell of all His wonders.
Glory in His holy name; let the hearts of those who seek the LORD rejoice.
Seek out the LORD and His strength; seek His face always.
Remember the {{niflaot|wonders}} He has done, His marvels, and the judgments He has pronounced,
O offspring of His servant Abraham, O sons of Jacob, His chosen ones.
He is the LORD our God; His judgments carry throughout the earth.
He remembers His {{berit|covenant}} forever, the word He ordained for a thousand generations,
the covenant He made with Abraham, and the oath He swore to Isaac.
He confirmed it to Jacob as a decree, to Israel as an everlasting covenant:
"I will give you the land of Canaan as the portion of your inheritance."

units.label: He rebuked kings on their behalf
units.note: the patriarchs protected among the nations

verses.text: When they were few in number, few indeed, and strangers in the land,
they wandered from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another.
He let no man oppress them; He rebuked kings on their behalf:
"Do not touch My {{mashiach|anointed ones}}! Do no harm to My prophets!"

units.label: He sent a man before them, Joseph

verses.text: He called down famine on the land and cut off all their supplies of food.
He sent a man before them, Joseph, sold as a slave.
They bruised his feet with shackles and placed his neck in irons,
until his prediction came true and the word of the LORD proved him right.
The king sent and released him; the ruler of peoples set him free.
He made him master of his household, ruler over all his substance,
to instruct his princes as he pleased and teach his elders wisdom.
Then Israel entered Egypt; Jacob dwelt in the land of Ham.
And the LORD made His people very fruitful, more numerous than their foes,
whose hearts He turned to hate His people, to conspire against His servants.
He sent Moses His servant, and Aaron, whom He had chosen.
They performed His miraculous signs among them, and wonders in the land of Ham.
He sent darkness, and it became dark, yet they defied His words.
He turned their waters to blood and caused their fish to die.
Their land teemed with frogs, even in their royal chambers.
He spoke, and insects swarmed, gnats throughout their country.
He gave them hail for rain, with lightning throughout their land.
He struck their vines and fig trees and shattered the trees of their country.
He spoke, and the locusts came, young locusts without number.
They devoured every plant in their land and consumed the produce of their soil.
Then He struck all the firstborn in their land, the firstfruits of all their vigor.

units.label: He brought Israel out with silver and gold

verses.text: He brought Israel out with silver and gold, and none among His tribes stumbled.
Egypt was glad when they departed, for the dread of Israel had fallen on them.
He spread a cloud as a covering and a fire to light up the night.
They asked, and He brought quail and satisfied them with the bread of heaven.
He opened a rock, and water gushed out; it flowed like a river in the desert.

units.label: That they might keep His statutes
units.note: the land given so that Israel might obey

verses.text: For He remembered His holy promise to Abraham His servant.
He brought forth His people with rejoicing, His chosen with shouts of joy.
He gave them the lands of the nations, that they might inherit the fruit of others' labor,
that they might keep His statutes and obey His laws. Hallelujah!

niflaot.gloss: Wonders, marvels, things beyond ordinary explanation. The psalm calls Israel to actively remember, not merely recall, these acts, keeping God's past faithfulness alive as present fuel for worship.

berit.gloss: Covenant, a binding agreement sworn by God Himself. The psalm anchors Israel's whole history, from Abraham to the conquest of Canaan, in this one unbreakable promise, kept for a thousand generations.

mashiach.gloss: Anointed one. Here it names the patriarchs themselves, set apart and protected by God among the nations; the same word later narrows to the one Anointed One, the Messiah, in whom God's protection of His people culminates.

basic.context: This psalm retells Israel's story from Abraham to the conquest of Canaan as one continuous act of God's covenant faithfulness. Its opening verses appear almost word for word in David's song when the ark was brought to Jerusalem, 1 Chronicles 16:8-22, showing it was treasured as a summary of Israel's identity: a people who exist because God remembered His promise.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm intentionally tells only one side of the story, God's faithfulness, and says almost nothing of Israel's failures; its companion, Psalm 106, supplies that other side, confessing the people's repeated rebellion. Read together, the pair displays grace to the utterly undeserving: God kept His word not because Israel earned it, but because He had sworn it.
basic.originalLanguages: Israel is called to actively remember, zakar, niflaot, God's wonders, verse 5, keeping the past alive as present worship. Everything rests on His berit, covenant, sworn to Abraham and confirmed to Isaac and Jacob, verses 8 to 10. Even the vulnerable patriarchs are called God's mashiach, His anointed ones, verse 15, under His direct protection.
basic.typology: Joseph, sold as a slave yet exalted to save the very people who wronged him, prefigures Christ, rejected by His own yet exalted to save them. The patriarchs called God's anointed ones, verse 15, anticipate the one true Anointed One, the Messiah, in whom God's protective covenant love finds its fullest expression.
basic.christ: Joseph's path from the pit and prison to the palace, where he saves the very family that betrayed him, is one of Scripture's clearest patterns of Christ: rejected, humbled, and exalted in order to save those who wronged Him, Acts 7:9-10, Genesis 50:20. Luke 1:72-73 shows Mary's song and Zechariah's prophecy both grounding Christ's coming in this same remembered covenant with Abraham.
basic.god: God is shown as utterly faithful to His own word across centuries and generations, protecting a handful of wandering strangers, turning betrayal into rescue through Joseph, humbling the greatest empire of the age through Moses and Aaron, and providing for His people's every need in a barren wilderness, all because He remembered His covenant.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Chronicles 16:8-22 preserves David's earlier version of this psalm's opening verses. Genesis 50:20 states Joseph's own theology of his suffering, you meant evil, but God meant it for good. Acts 7:9-17 retells this same history in Stephen's speech. Luke 1:72-73 grounds the incarnation in God's remembered oath to Abraham.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's rehearsal of covenant faithfulness, kept across centuries of famine, slavery, and wilderness, is the story that Christ Himself fulfills and completes, the promised seed of Abraham in whom all the families of the earth are blessed, Galatians 3:16, Luke 1:72-73.

context.literary:
The psalm has two halves of unequal size. Verses 1 to 6 are a rapid fire of commands addressed to 'the offspring of His servant Abraham': give thanks, call, make known, sing, tell, glory, seek, seek, remember. Verses 7 to 45 then supply the reasons, as a single sweep of narrative. In the first half Israel acts; in the second, almost everything is done by God. The grammar of the history is that God is the subject of nearly every sentence, and Israel is the one who is protected, enriched, led and fed.

Within the narrative, a verb carries the story: 'sent.' God 'sent a man before them, Joseph' (verse 17); then 'the king sent and released him' (verse 20), the king using the same verb; then God 'sent Moses His servant' (verse 26), and 'sent darkness' (verse 28). The repeated verb says that every move in the history, including the deliverance Pharaoh himself performs for Joseph, is part of one sending.

The shape of the middle is a series of small movements. Verses 12 to 15 show the patriarchs wandering and protected. Verses 16 to 22 follow Joseph from famine to shackles to the palace. Verses 23 to 25 move Israel into Egypt and into trouble. Verses 26 to 36 narrate the plagues. Verses 37 to 41 describe the departure and the wilderness. Verses 42 to 45 return to the promise with which the history began, in verses 8 to 11, so that the narrative is framed by Abraham: the covenant remembered at the start and 'His holy promise to Abraham His servant' at the end.

The selection is as telling as the content. The psalm mentions eight plagues and puts darkness first, though Exodus places it ninth. It leaves out the boils and the death of livestock. And it moves from the wilderness straight to the land with no word of Sinai, the golden calf or any of Israel's failures. This is deliberate. The psalm shows only one side of the history, the side God himself wrote, and it ends on the purpose of the whole thing: 'that they might keep His statutes and obey His laws.' The last word is 'Hallelujah.'
context.historical:
The first fifteen verses appear, with small differences, in David's song of thanksgiving when the ark was brought to Jerusalem, 1 Chronicles 16:8-22. The psalm as it stands extends that song through the whole history to the conquest. It sits in Book IV of the Psalter, which was shaped around the experience of exile, and Psalm 106 ends with a prayer, 'Save us, O LORD our God, and gather us from the nations' (106:47). The first hearers may therefore have been a people scattered or recently regathered who needed to remember how they began.

That beginning is the point. When the promise was made to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, they were 'few in number, few indeed, and strangers in the land' (verse 12), wanderers who passed from kingdom to kingdom. Deuteronomy 26:5 had taught every Israelite to say at the harvest offering, 'My father was a wandering Aramean, and he went down to Egypt few in number.' Israel after the exile was small, dependent on Persian goodwill and surrounded by neighbours, and the psalm tells them that smallness is where God's promises began.

The details in verses 14 and 15 draw on Genesis. The LORD struck Pharaoh with plagues because of Sarah, Genesis 12:17, and warned Abimelech in a dream, Genesis 20:3; and called Abraham 'a prophet,' Genesis 20:7. Genesis 35:5 records the terror from God that kept the cities from pursuing Jacob's sons. In verses 16 to 22 the psalm summarizes Joseph's story, from the famine, to the pit and prison, Genesis 37:28 and 39:20, to the court of Pharaoh, Genesis 41:38-45. The 430 years in Egypt (Exodus 12:40) are compressed into three verses, 23 to 25, because the psalm's interest is not in the length of the stay but in the God who multiplied them there.

'The land of Ham' (verses 23 and 27) is a poetic name for Egypt, reaching back to the table of nations where Ham's son Mizraim is the ancestor of Egypt, Genesis 10:6. The silver and gold of verse 37 recall the gifts the Egyptians gave when Israel asked, Exodus 12:35-36, the payment God had promised Abraham in Genesis 15:14.
context.canonical:
Psalm 105 belongs to a small family of 'history psalms': 78, 105, 106, 135 and 136. Each retells Israel's story to teach something. Psalm 78 tells it as a warning about forgetting, Psalm 106 as a confession of sin, and Psalm 136 as a litany, 'His loving devotion endures forever.' Psalm 105 tells it as a song of the faithfulness of God, and in the Psalter it is paired with 106 so that the two halves of the story, grace and failure, can be read in order. Psalm 106:7 says of the same events, 'Our fathers in Egypt did not grasp Your wonders,' the other side of Psalm 105's wonders.

The psalm leans on Genesis and Exodus. Its covenant language is taken from the promises to Abraham, Genesis 12:1-3 and 17:7-8, and its description of a covenant kept for a thousand generations matches Deuteronomy 7:9. The land that Israel inherits 'from the labour of others' (verse 44) is the land of Deuteronomy 6:10-11 and Joshua 24:13, where houses are filled that Israel did not build.

The New Testament takes the psalm in several ways. Stephen retells the same history in Acts 7, with Joseph's sale, rescue and elevation told in 7:9 and 10 and the key phrase, 'On their second visit, Joseph revealed his identity to his brothers,' in 7:13, which Stephen uses to point to Jesus whom Israel rejected. The song of Zechariah and Mary's Magnificat in Luke 1 base the coming of Christ on the oath to Abraham, Luke 1:72-73. Paul argues from the same covenant that the promise was given before the law, Galatians 3:16-17, and that all who belong to Christ are Abraham's seed, Galatians 3:29. Paul also treats the cloud, the sea, the spiritual food and the rock as events written for our instruction, 1 Corinthians 10:1-4, and Hebrews 11:22 notes that Joseph spoke by faith of the exodus.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wanted Israel to understand their own survival. A tiny family had wandered between kingdoms, a favourite son had been sold, a whole people had been enslaved, and yet each time something unexpected happened. Kings were warned, a slave became a ruler, an empire was broken. The explanation he offers is one sentence: 'He remembers His covenant forever' (verse 8). The nation did not outlast the odds by strength, and its history was not luck.

He also meant the psalm to produce a particular kind of worship. The opening commands are unusually active. Israel is to give thanks, but also to 'make known His deeds among the nations' and to 'seek His face always.' Remembering is not a private feeling; it is public speech. The people who tell what God has done are, by telling it, drawn to seek Him.

Finally, the closing verse explains why the gifts were given. God brought them out with joy and gave them the land 'that they might keep His statutes and obey His laws.' The psalmist expects a people formed by grace to be formed for obedience. Saved people are meant to live differently, and the last word of the psalm, 'Hallelujah,' means the obedience is joyful. A reader who had spent years in exile would hear it as a call to start again on the same footing: remember the promise, then keep the law.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm records what God did in specific events, and not everything it narrates is a pattern for us to copy. The plagues were a judgment on Egypt at a unique moment; they are not a template for how God deals with nations now. The land given in verse 44 is the land of Canaan, given to Israel under the covenant, and the phrase 'the fruit of others' labor' describes what happened in that historic act. It is not permission for any group to take land by force in God's name. Scripture itself limits that moment: Deuteronomy 9:4-5 says the nations were driven out for their wickedness and not for Israel's righteousness.

In the same way, 'Do not touch My anointed ones! Do no harm to My prophets!' (verse 15) describes God's protection of the patriarchs in a particular season. It is not a general rule that leaders are beyond criticism. What does apply directly are the imperatives of verses 1 to 5: give thanks, sing, tell, seek, remember. These are meant for every reader. The purpose clause of verse 45 also carries over: those who have received God's gifts are to keep His commands. And the thread of the psalm, that God keeps His promises, is to be received as comfort and as a basis for trust.

debates.question: Why does the psalm leave out Sinai and Israel's sin?

views.label: It is a hymn of praise, and Psalm 106 supplies the confession
views.case: Psalms 105 and 106 are paired. The first narrates what God did, and the second what Israel did. Singing the first without the second would give a lopsided history, so the pair is meant to be read together. Psalm 106:7, for example, takes up the same Egyptian events from the side of Israel's failure.

views.label: The emphasis is on the promise to Abraham as prior to the law
views.case: The psalm frames its history with the covenant with Abraham (verses 8 to 11 and 42), not with the covenant at Sinai. Paul makes a similar point in Galatians 3:17, that the law came 430 years later and does not cancel the earlier promise. The psalm ends with statutes and laws, so they are not ignored, but they appear as the purpose of grace rather than its basis.

views.label: The silence is a rhetorical choice for a discouraged audience
views.case: A people in exile, convinced they had forfeited everything, needed to hear that the story began with God's faithfulness. The omission of their failures is not denial, since they already knew them, but a way of making the point that God's commitment never depended on their record.

debates.bearing: The silence is not a claim that Israel was faithful. It is a choice to let the covenant promise be heard first, and it makes the grace in the story clearer.

debates.question: What does it mean that God 'turned' the Egyptians' hearts to hate Israel (verse 25)?

views.label: God used Egypt's existing fear and pride, working through human choices
views.case: Exodus 1 shows Pharaoh acting from fear of Israel's numbers. The psalm credits God with the outcome without erasing the Egyptians' responsibility. Rulers choose hatred, and God, who rules over all, uses it to move His people out.

views.label: God actively directs even hostile hearts
views.case: The verb is active: God turned their hearts. Exodus 4:21 and 7:3 say God would harden Pharaoh's heart, and Romans 9:17-18 draws the conclusion that God has mercy on whom He wills and hardens whom He wills. On this reading the psalm shows God's sovereignty extends to the hearts of His enemies.

views.label: The statement describes God's purposes, not a coercion of the unwilling
views.case: Many readers hold that the biblical language of hardening describes God confirming a direction people have already chosen. The psalm is interested not in the mechanism but in the claim that even the people's oppression fell within God's plan, as Joseph says in Genesis 50:20.

debates.bearing: All three views agree that Egypt's hatred was no accident outside God's reach. The psalm uses it to show that God's covenant could not be undone even by an empire's malice.

debates.question: Who 'defied His words' in verse 28?

views.label: The Egyptians defied God's words
views.case: The BSB reads 'yet they defied His words' and places it right after the darkness, so that the line comments on Pharaoh's court refusing to heed even this sign. That fits Exodus, where the king repeatedly refuses to let the people go.

views.label: Moses and Aaron did not defy God's words
views.case: Many English versions render the line as a statement that the two servants did not rebel against His words. The previous verse has them performing His signs, so the sentence can be read as a note on their obedience.

views.label: The line is uncertain and the point stands either way
views.case: The BSB footnote says its wording rests on the Greek and Syriac, while the Hebrew is worded as a question, 'had they not defied His words?' With witnesses this tangled, the sensible course is to hold the reading loosely.

debates.bearing: The uncertainty is a reminder to hold such a line loosely. The sure teaching comes from the parts of the psalm that are not in dispute.

study.originalLanguages:
The psalm opens with a small puzzle when set beside 1 Chronicles 16. Where David's song says 'Remember His covenant forever,' an instruction, Psalm 105:8 says 'He remembers His covenant forever,' a statement. Chronicles tells Israel what to do; the psalm tells Israel what God does. The one is the human response and the other its ground, and together they cover the whole relationship.

The word for 'strangers' in verse 12 is ger, the resident alien without land or standing. It is the word Moses uses when he reminds Israel to love the foreigner 'for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt,' Leviticus 19:34. Israel's identity begins as ger, the people who owned nothing and were kept by God, and this is part of why Israel is commanded to protect the vulnerable.

Verse 16 says God 'cut off all their supplies of food.' The Hebrew, as the BSB footnote shows, is 'staff,' and the phrase is that He broke the staff of bread. Bread is pictured as the staff that holds up a person's life; when it breaks, the whole body falls. Leviticus 26:26 and Ezekiel 4:16 use similar language for famine.

The most striking word is in verse 19. The BSB translates 'the word of the LORD proved him right,' but the verb is tsaraph, which in the Old Testament is the verb of the refiner at the furnace, as in Psalm 66:10, 'You refined us like silver.' Joseph's own prediction came true, but it was the LORD's word that tested him, and the preceding verse tells us the iron was on his neck. Hebrew can use nephesh for 'neck' or 'throat' as well as 'soul,' so older English versions spoke of iron entering his soul. The picture is of a man held in a furnace until the word of God had done its work in him.

The verb 'sent' is shalach, used four times in the psalm in a way that gathers the whole story. God sent Joseph (verse 17), the king sent and released him (verse 20), God sent Moses (verse 26) and sent darkness (verse 28). Joseph himself used it in Genesis 45:5 and 7, 'God sent me before you.' The psalm shares his reading.

In verse 25 the verb 'turned' is haphak, a verb that means to turn over or reverse. Hearts are overturned so that welcome becomes hatred. In verse 39 the cloud is a 'covering,' masak, a word used elsewhere of the screen at the door of the tabernacle. The cloud over Israel is a screen as well as a sign.

Finally, verse 45 ends with the 'statutes' (chuqqim) and 'laws' (torot), the plural of torah. The final goal of rescue is a people who live by torah, and the last word, 'Hallelujah,' turns that goal into praise.

typology.type: Joseph, sent ahead, humbled and exalted, verses 16 to 22
typology.fulfillment: Joseph is sold by his brothers for silver, thrown into prison, and then raised by Pharaoh to rule, so that he may feed the very family that wronged him. Stephen draws the line to Jesus in Acts 7: 'On their second visit, Joseph revealed his identity to his brothers,' Acts 7:13, and later charges his hearers with being the 'betrayers and murderers' of the Righteous One, Acts 7:52. Peter says the same in Acts 3:13-15: the God of Abraham 'glorified His servant Jesus,' whom they killed and God raised. The parallel is strong, since both were rejected, sold, suffered unjustly, and were exalted in order to save. It also falls short: Joseph saved lives in a famine, while Christ saves from sin and death, and He did so by dying.

God brings His people out with rejoicing, plunder, and no one stumbling. The New Testament calls Jesus' death an exodus. On the mountain Moses and Elijah spoke with Him about 'His departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem,' Luke 9:31, a word that in Greek is exodus. His people are brought out of the dominion of darkness, Colossians 1:13, and the Passover lamb becomes the pattern for Christ. The earlier exodus freed a nation from Pharaoh, and the later frees people from sin, but both are acts of a God who remembers a promise.

typology.type: The cloud, the bread and the rock, verses 39 to 41
typology.fulfillment: God covers them with a cloud, feeds them with bread from heaven, and opens a rock for water. Jesus says, 'it is My Father who gives you the true bread from heaven,' John 6:32, and 'I am the bread of life,' John 6:35. He offers living water to the thirsty, John 7:37-38, and calls Himself 'the light of the world,' John 8:12. Paul says the Israelites 'drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ,' 1 Corinthians 10:4. The wilderness gifts are real provisions in their own right; in Christ they become signs of the deeper provision that satisfies the soul.

typology.type: The land as inheritance, verses 11, 42 to 45
typology.fulfillment: The promise to Abraham is a land given as an inheritance. Hebrews 11:9-10 says Abraham lived as a stranger in tents because he was looking for 'the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God,' and Hebrews 4:8-9 says that if Joshua had given rest, another day would not be spoken of, so a Sabbath rest remains. Peter describes believers' inheritance as 'imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven,' 1 Peter 1:4, and Paul says the Spirit is the pledge of that inheritance, Ephesians 1:13-14. The land was a true gift, but in Christ the promise grows into a world and a rest that cannot be lost.

study.christ:
Luke begins his Gospel with two songs that quote this psalm's logic. Zechariah says that God has acted 'to show mercy to our fathers and to remember His holy covenant, the oath He swore to our father Abraham,' Luke 1:72-73, and Mary sings that He has helped Israel, 'remembering to be merciful, as He promised to our fathers, to Abraham and his descendants forever,' Luke 1:54-55. That is Psalm 105:8 to 11 and 42 in the mouths of people who are watching it fulfilled. The God who remembered Abraham in Egypt remembers him again in a manger. The psalm teaches us to read the coming of Jesus not as a break with the old story but as the arrival of the thing it was promising all along.

Paul reads the promise with the same weight. When the covenant words speak of Abraham 'and his seed,' he says, the Scripture 'does not say, "and to seeds," meaning many, but "and to your seed," meaning One, who is Christ,' Galatians 3:16. He also notes that the law came 430 years later and does not cancel the earlier promise, Galatians 3:17. So the covenant of verses 8 to 11, which God 'ordained for a thousand generations,' is ultimately a covenant that finds its yes in Christ: 'all the promises of God are "Yes" in Christ,' 2 Corinthians 1:20.

The pattern of Joseph in verses 16 to 22 is the clearest pointer. Stephen tells how Joseph was rejected by his brothers, then made known to them the second time, Acts 7:13. In Acts 3:13-15 Peter charges the people with rejecting 'the Holy and Righteous One' whom God raised. Joseph's own explanation, that what his brothers intended for evil 'God intended for good,' to 'preserve the lives of many people,' Genesis 50:20, becomes in the New Testament the explanation of the cross: what men meant for evil, God used for the rescue of many. The comparison is not a point-by-point allegory, and the New Testament does not use Joseph's coat or cupbearers as codes. The main shape of the story is what matters: the one sent ahead, rejected, humbled, then raised to feed those who rejected him.

The provision in the wilderness also points forward. The bread from heaven is given a meaning by Jesus: 'I am the bread of life,' John 6:35. The rock that flowed with water was, Paul says, Christ, 1 Corinthians 10:4. And the cloud and fire that led Israel give way to the one who says, 'Whoever follows Me will never walk in the darkness,' John 8:12.

Finally, the exodus itself becomes the pattern for Christ's own work. Moses and Elijah talk with Jesus about His 'departure,' which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem, Luke 9:31, and the Greek word there is exodus. Christ leads His people out, and what began with silver and gold ends with a better inheritance.
study.god:
The one idea that holds this psalm together is that God remembers. Verse 8 says, 'He remembers His covenant forever,' and verse 42 says, 'He remembered His holy promise to Abraham His servant.' Memory in Scripture is not recall but commitment. When God remembers, He acts. The story from Abraham to Canaan is a record of what God's remembering looks like across centuries.

He is faithful across time. The covenant was spoken to a childless man and sworn to a thousand generations. Between the promise and the land there was a famine, a slave market, a prison, a hostile king, ten plagues and a wilderness. God's faithfulness was not tested by an easy path. It is the mark of this God that He is patient with timing: Genesis 15:13 told Abraham the long delay in advance, and Exodus 12:41 notes the exodus came 'to the very day.'

He is sovereign over rulers. The psalm says He rebuked kings on behalf of the patriarchs, gave Joseph favour in Pharaoh's court, turned the Egyptians' hearts, and sent plagues that Pharaoh could not stop. Kings appear as characters in God's story, never as its authors. Yet this is not a blunt power: it is directed at His people's good, and it is applied with restraint, as when the plagues are called 'signs' and 'wonders' that reveal who He is.

He is just. Egypt's judgment follows Egypt's cruelty, and Genesis 15:14 had said God would judge the nation that enslaved Israel. Verse 36 records the death of the firstborn without comment, and verse 44 records the gift of lands taken from nations. The psalm does not defend these acts; it names them as the acts of the God who judges, and it is silent about the Canaanites' guilt, which Deuteronomy 9:4-5 supplies. It also shows how deeply He cares for those He rescues. Verse 37 says 'none among His tribes stumbled.' He brings them out rich, healthy and rejoicing.

He is provider. The cloud covers them from the sun and gives light at night, quail and bread satisfy them, the rock gives water 'like a river in the desert.' The wilderness is a place without resources, and the psalm treats it as a place where God's hand is most visible.

He is purposeful. The purpose in verse 45 is that His people keep His laws. God does not rescue simply for the sake of rescue; He rescues a people to be His own and to reflect His character.

For worship, the psalm reminds us that praise has content. We do not praise a vague goodness, but the God who did these particular things for these particular people. To 'make known His deeds among the nations' is to tell the story.

crossReferences.note: David's song when the ark came to Jerusalem contains the same opening fifteen verses with small changes. Where Chronicles says 'Remember His covenant,' the psalm says 'He remembers.' The overlap shows this praise was already old and loved when the longer psalm was composed.

God's first promise to Abraham of a great nation, a blessing and a name. Psalm 105 retells all of Israel's history as the long working out of this promise, and shows that every danger on the way was met by the God who spoke it.

God tells Abraham that his descendants will be strangers, enslaved for four hundred years, and then will leave with great possessions. Psalm 105:23 to 25 and 37 are that prophecy kept, down to the silver and gold.

Joseph tells his brothers, 'God sent me before you.' The psalm adopts his word 'sent' in verse 17 and makes it the key to the history. What the brothers meant as betrayal was, from God's side, a sending.

Joseph says that what his brothers meant for evil, God meant for good, to preserve many lives. It states the theology behind Psalm 105:16 to 22, and is the Old Testament's clearest statement that God can bring rescue out of human wrong without excusing it.

The Israelites ask the Egyptians for silver, gold and clothing and the LORD gives them favor so they are given it. This is the event behind Psalm 105:37, which says God brought them out with silver and gold.

The companion psalm says that in Egypt the fathers 'did not grasp Your wonders or remember Your abundant kindness.' Psalm 105 tells what God did, and Psalm 106 shows how little Israel understood, so that grace appears all the greater.

Stephen retells Joseph's story, from jealous brothers to rescue to second revelation. He uses the history of Psalm 105 to accuse Israel of repeating the brothers' pattern and rejecting the one God had sent.

Zechariah says God acts to remember His holy covenant, the oath to Abraham. It is Psalm 105:8, 9 and 42 in the mouth of a prophet who sees the covenant promise fulfilled in the child about to be born.

Paul argues that the promise was to Abraham's seed, 'meaning One, who is Christ,' and that the law 430 years later does not cancel it. It supplies the reading of Psalm 105's Abrahamic framing that the New Testament gives.
Paul points to the cloud, the sea, the spiritual food and the rock and says the rock was Christ. It reads Psalm 105:39 to 41 as the provision of a God whose provision, in the end, is Christ Himself.

God will bring Israel into a land with cities they did not build and wells they did not dig. It is the background to Psalm 105:44, 'the fruit of others' labor,' and a reminder that the inheritance was a gift, which Israel was to receive with gratitude and obedience.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 12 begins with a promise made to a man with no heir: a land, a nation, a blessing for all families. Everything that follows is a test of whether that promise will hold. Psalm 105 is a victory lap taken in advance: it says it held, through famine, slavery, empire and desert. Where Genesis 3 recorded what humanity lost, this psalm records what God kept. The covenant sworn to Abraham is the one thread that no catastrophe cut.

In the psalm's own setting it also answers a later crisis. A people who had lost land and temple needed to hear that they had begun smaller, in a worse position, and that God had still done what He promised. The history is told to those in exile, and it suggests that their return is also within the promise. The prophets said the same thing: Jeremiah 29:10 and Isaiah 44:26-28 promised restoration, and Psalm 106:47 asks for it.

The story reaches its centre in Christ. The seed to whom the promise was spoken is Christ, Galatians 3:16, and His coming is said to be God's remembering the covenant, Luke 1:72-73. The pattern of Joseph, rejected and raised to save, finds its fullest form in Him. The exodus is the pattern of His work, Luke 9:31. The bread, rock and cloud find their meaning in Him, John 6:35 and 1 Corinthians 10:4. And the land of verse 11 widens into what Paul calls being 'heir of the world,' Romans 4:13, shared by all who belong to Christ, Galatians 3:29.

The psalm points beyond its own end. It closes with a land and a law but no rest, and the writer of Hebrews notes that Joshua did not finally give rest, so 'there remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God,' Hebrews 4:8-9. In the new creation the inheritance is complete: the city with foundations whose builder is God, Hebrews 11:10, the dwelling of God with His people, Revelation 21:3. The people who set out as strangers 'few in number' end as a company no one can count, Revelation 7:9, praising the God who remembered. The final 'Hallelujah' of Psalm 105 is a rehearsal for theirs.

quiz.q: What does the psalm call Israel to do in verse 5?

options.text: Remember the wonders He has done, His marvels, and the judgments He has pronounced.
options.note: Active remembrance of God's past faithfulness is the engine of the psalm's praise.

options.text: Forget the past and focus only on the present.
options.note: The psalm's entire structure is built on remembering, not forgetting, God's past acts.

options.text: Build a monument to Abraham in Canaan.
options.note: No monument is mentioned; the call is to remember, not to construct a physical memorial.

options.text: Consult the prophets for a new word from God.
options.note: Prophets are mentioned in verse 15 as protected by God, not as the object of the call in verse 5, which is to remember His past wonders.

quiz.q: What did God do for the patriarchs while they were few in number and strangers in the land, verses 12-15?

options.text: He let no man oppress them and rebuked kings on their behalf.
options.note: God's protection over the vulnerable patriarchs, seen in Genesis 12, 20, and 26, shows His covenant faithfulness even before Israel existed as a nation.

options.text: He commanded them to build fortified cities immediately.
options.note: The text shows God Himself protecting them, not a command to build defenses.

options.text: He allowed foreign kings to enslave them for a time.
options.note: The text says the opposite, God rebuked kings and let no man oppress them.

options.text: He sent angels to fight physical battles for them.
options.note: The text specifically names God's rebuke of kings, not angelic warfare, as the means of protection here.

quiz.q: How did Joseph end up ruling in Egypt, according to verses 17-22?

options.text: He was sold as a slave, imprisoned, and then released and exalted by the king.
options.note: The psalm compresses Joseph's whole account, sold, imprisoned, and finally exalted to master his household and instruct princes.

options.text: He was born into Pharaoh's royal family.
options.note: The text explicitly says he was sold as a slave, not born into Egyptian royalty.

options.text: He led a military conquest of Egypt.
options.note: Joseph's rise came through interpretation of dreams and administrative wisdom, not military conquest.

options.text: He purchased his freedom with his own wealth.
options.note: The text says the king sent and released him; it was the king's action, not Joseph purchasing his own freedom.

quiz.q: What was the stated purpose of God giving Israel the lands of the nations, verses 44-45?

options.text: That they might keep His statutes and obey His laws.
options.note: The gift of the land was never an end in itself; it was given so Israel would live in grateful obedience to God.

options.text: That they might become wealthier than all other nations.
options.note: The stated purpose is obedience to God's statutes, not accumulation of wealth for its own sake.

options.text: That they might build a great army to conquer further territory.
options.note: The psalm names obedience to God's law as the purpose, not further military conquest.

options.text: That they might forget their history in Egypt.
options.note: The whole psalm is built around remembering, not forgetting, God's past dealings with them.

quiz.q: How does Joseph's story in this psalm point toward Christ?

options.text: Joseph was rejected and humbled by his own family yet exalted to save them, prefiguring Christ's rejection, humbling, and exaltation to save those who wronged Him.
options.note: Compare Acts 7:9-10 and Genesis 50:20; the pattern of betrayal turned to salvation runs from Joseph to Christ.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ at all.
options.note: Scripture itself draws this connection, notably in Stephen's speech in Acts 7 and in the pattern of rejection followed by exaltation.

options.text: It predicts the exact geography of Christ's ministry.
options.note: The connection is thematic, rejection turned to salvation, not a matter of predicted geography.

options.text: It shows that suffering always leads to earthly wealth.
options.note: The point is not a formula for material prosperity but the pattern of God turning betrayal into rescue for others.

questions: The psalm calls Israel to actively remember God's wonders, verse 5, not merely to know facts about them. What has God done in your own life that you need to deliberately remember and retell this week?

God protected the patriarchs when they were few, vulnerable, and strangers in the land, verses 12-15. Where do you feel small or exposed right now, and how does God's care for Abraham's family speak to that?

Joseph's suffering, verses 17-19, came before his exaltation, and his own verdict on it was, God meant it for good, Genesis 50:20. What painful chapter of your story might God be using in ways you cannot yet see?

The psalm insists twice that God acted because He remembered His covenant, verses 8 and 42, not because Israel earned it. Where are you tempted to think God's favor toward you depends on your performance rather than His promise?

This psalm is deliberately paired with Psalm 106's confession of failure. How does holding both truths together, God's faithfulness and our unfaithfulness, shape a more honest and grateful kind of praise?

The land was given so that Israel might keep God's statutes, verse 45, not as an end in itself. What blessings has God given you that you have treated as ends in themselves rather than as calls to grateful obedience?

translationNotes.note: Supplies of food renders a Hebrew word literally meaning staff, a picture of the support that sustains life, here cut off by the famine that sends Joseph's family toward Egypt.
To instruct in verse 22 follows the Septuagint and Syriac; the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads to bind, likely reflecting the same underlying idea of Joseph exercising authority over Pharaoh's officials.

Yet they defied His words follows the Septuagint and Syriac; the Hebrew reads more literally, for had they not defied His words, a difficult clause either way pointing to Egypt's continued resistance under the plagues.
